mainEntity.name: How is a penetration test different from a security scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A scan looks for known patterns, automatically. A manual test asks which findings someone can actually use, and probes the logic that's specific to your app, permissions, payments and the rest. We use automated tools during a test too. We just don't hand you their raw output and call it a report.
It's the public standard for scoring how severe a vulnerability is, from 0 to 10. It helps your team decide what gets fixed first.
Once. We go back over the findings we reported and check whether they're actually fixed. Anything new, or changed since, needs a new test.

Nothing gets tested before three documents are signed

items: Written scope: exactly which domains, apps, APIs and accounts are in, and which are out, in what time window, and with which methods.
Letter of Authorisation: the system's legal owner gives written permission to test.
Non-disclosure agreement (NDA): whatever we find, and any data we see along the way, stays confidential.

blocks.html: Missing even one of the three? Then we don't test. Not even a quick trial.
Penetration testing

Better you hear it from us than from a stranger. We test your web app or API by hand, under a signed scope, score what we find, and retest after your fixes. And if by security you mean your shop's Instagram page, start here: your shop page got hacked? Do these things first.
A scanner won't tell you this
If your web app or API handles people's data or their payments, the question isn't whether you have weak spots. It's which of them can actually be used, and what someone reaches once they're through.

An automated scan can't answer that. It hands you a long list of warnings, half of them noise. The opposite failure is just as common: a report that says "secure" without ever saying what was tested, which is comfort you can't rely on. So teams end up either buried in warnings nobody prioritised, or reassured by a piece of paper that proves very little.

We're Roxana Negaresh and Arshia Amani. We test by hand, and only under a scope signed before anything starts, with the authorisation letter and NDA beside it. Every finding comes with a CVSS score, the evidence, what it lets someone do, and how to fix it, and retesting those findings is included in the price. One thing we'll say plainly now: no test proves complete security, and we don't write certificates claiming it does.
This is for teams who

items: You run a web app or API that handles user data, payments or anything sensitive.
A customer or partner wants to see a security test report before they'll sign with you.
You want one sensitive feature, login, payments, the admin panel, tested properly before launch.

blocks.html: We will turn you down if

items: The system isn't yours and you don't hold the owner's written authorisation.
You want a certificate saying "fully secure" or "zero vulnerabilities". No test proves that. We won't write it.
All you want is an automated scanner run and its raw output handed over.
You need social engineering, physical testing, or internal network infrastructure testing.

blocks.html: From signature to retest

items: Scope. Input: a conversation about your system and its risks. Output: the signed written scope, Letter of Authorisation and NDA. Owner: you and dadmor.

Test. Input: the signed scope and test accounts. Output: findings, with evidence. Method: PTES for structure, OWASP WSTG for the web work, and the OWASP Top 10 and API Security Top 10 where they apply. Owner: dadmor.
Report. Input: the findings. Output: two reports, one for executives and one technical, every finding carrying its CVSS score, evidence, impact and fix. Owner: dadmor.
Fix. Input: the report. Output: the fixes, in your system. Owner: your team.
Retest. Input: the fixes you tell us are done. Output: one retest of the findings we reported, and an updated status report. Owner: dadmor, inside the window the scope sets.

blocks.html: Deliverables
What makes a test bigger

items: What sets the size: how many apps, APIs and endpoints, how many user roles (guest, user, admin), and how much business logic needs testing, payments and permissions especially.
From you: a test environment, or written permission to test production, test accounts for every role, one technical contact, and the three signed documents.
What delays a test: authorisation signed late, test accounts that don't work, and an environment that changes mid-test.

blocks.html: How it's priced

items: There's no band to pick from here. You get a fixed-scope proposal after we talk, and one retest of the reported findings is included.

blocks.html: Read this part twice

items: A test covers what was in scope, at the moment it ran. Anything outside the scope, and anything changed afterwards, wasn't checked, and the report says so openly.
Finding nothing means this test found nothing. It doesn't mean nothing exists.
Testing production carries risk, downtime or changed data. High-risk techniques run only with written approval, at a time we agree on.
Fixing what we find is your team's job, unless we scope the fixing separately.
